items.statement: Fewer people call themselves atheists after a DMT 'being' encounter, and after drug-free 'God' encounters too.
items.why: Among people who'd had such meetings, 28 in 100 recalled being atheists before a DMT encounter and 10 in 100 said they were now, and the share fell without drugs too. But they were recalling old beliefs years later.

items.statement: Most volunteers in one lab study ranked a single psilocybin session among their 5 most meaningful experiences.
items.why: Two months later, 67 in 100 did. But everyone in that study already took part in religious or spiritual activities, which may have made them see it as more spiritual.

items.statement: A meth overdose shows up as slow breathing and tiny pupils.
items.why: It's the reverse: it looks like a body in overdrive, with a racing heart, fast breathing, wide pupils and great restlessness. That's second-hand, from two reviews of hospital studies, and how often each sign shows up varies a lot.

items.statement: The more traditional the ayahuasca ceremony, the less fear people feel.
items.why: In one big survey, more traditional practices went with a little more fear, and church hymns or sermons with less. The differences were small, and people rated everything looking back.

items.statement: Lots of people who take magic mushrooms end up seeking emergency treatment.
items.why: In one big online survey, about 2 in 1,000 people who'd used them in the past year said they had, and nearly all of those felt back to normal within a day. But nobody checked their answers, and anyone who couldn't answer wasn't counted.

items.statement: Other people's cannabis smoke can never make you fail a urine drug test.
items.why: After an hour in a sealed, smoky room, 1 of 18 people who didn't smoke went over the US government's workplace limit, and 12 tested positive at least once at a lower limit some private tests use. That was one small lab test, mostly in thick smoke, not everyday smoke.

items.statement: In lab tests, fentanyl test strips often missed fentanyl that was really there.
items.why: Strips showed fentanyl in 104 of 106 police-seized samples that had it. But trained lab staff did the tests, mostly with one brand, and testing at home wasn't studied.

items.statement: One ketamine drip can lift depression within hours.
items.why: A day after one drip, 64 in 100 were much better, against 28 in 100 after a sedative drip. But for most the lift faded within weeks, and people can often tell they got ketamine, which may make it look bigger.

items.statement: In a big trial for hard-to-treat depression, psilocybin's benefit was still clear after 12 weeks.
items.why: By 12 weeks, the gap with the comparison group could be chance. People could probably tell they'd taken psilocybin, and nobody checked, which may have made the earlier gap look bigger.

items.statement: Teens who remembered more of the US government's anti-drug ads were, if anything, more likely to try cannabis.
items.why: In a national survey, they were no less likely to start, fewer said they definitely wouldn't, and in one of three periods more ads went with more first use. The authors call that tentative, not definitive.

items.statement: In older US surveys, about 9 in 100 people who ever tried cannabis became dependent.
items.why: In the first survey, that was fewer than for tobacco, heroin, cocaine or alcohol. The surveys ran from 1990 to 2005 and used a narrower definition; newer US figures that count milder cases are higher.

items.statement: Almost everyone who tries stimulants like meth gets hooked.
items.why: It depends how you count: an old US survey found about 11 in 100 had ever been dependent, and a broader Australian count estimated about 50 in 100 within 14 years. Neither had a number for meth alone.

items.statement: In UK reports, most people with low blood salt after MDMA had drunk a lot of liquid.
items.why: At least 10 of 17 cases reported to a UK poisons service had, and the 2 who died had brain swelling. These reports count only people who got ill, so they can't show how often it happens or whether drinking more changes the risk.

items.statement: If a friend took the same MDMA and didn't overheat, you won't either.
items.why: Nobody can yet say why some people get hotter than others: in one case of severe overheating, a friend who took the same MDMA didn't overheat. That's second-hand, from one review of small studies and cases.

items.statement: Most men who used cannabis heavily never went to hospital with schizophrenia, in a big Swedish study.
items.why: About 38 in 1,000 men who'd used it more than 50 times later did, against about 6 in 1,000 who had never used it. These counts don't allow for other differences between the men.

items.statement: Weed really is stronger than it used to be, on average.
items.why: Across 7 countries from 1970 to 2017, THC, its main active part, rose about 3 points every 10 years in weed and 6 in hash. But most samples were seized by police, so they may not match what people buy.

items.statement: Teen cannabis use has been shown to lower IQ later in life.
items.why: In one New Zealand study, people dependent on it for years lost about 6 points from their childhood scores. Another researcher showed family background could produce a similar pattern; the first team found it didn't change their result.

items.statement: On average, people who often use cannabis score a little lower on memory tests.
items.why: A big review found small gaps in learning, memory, attention and planning, but none clear for language, shape or movement. People were tested only after they'd started, so it can't show cannabis caused the gap.

items.reason: Dull for a myth-or-fact card: a medicine beating a dummy pill is no surprise, and the trials say little about people using heroin or on methadone or buprenorphine.

items.statement: The 2002 study claiming ecstasy harmed monkeys' brains had actually given the animals a different drug.
items.why: The drug came from a wrongly labelled bottle, and the study was withdrawn a year later. The withdrawal notice doesn't say what the one animal that got ecstasy showed.

items.statement: All antidepressants carry about the same serotonin risk when mixed with ecstasy.
items.why: One 2007 review ranked MAOI antidepressants highest and SSRI-type antidepressants lower. That's the authors' judgment from reports and how the drugs work; no study counted how often each mix causes harm.

items.statement: Worldwide, alcohol is estimated to cause millions of deaths a year.
items.why: Global models put it at about 2.3 to 2.8 million a year, against a world where no one drank, and at ages 15 to 49 it was the top risk factor in one study. These are computer estimates, not counted deaths.

items.statement: In a UK expert ranking of 20 drugs, tobacco scored zero for deaths like overdose.
items.why: Lung cancer was counted elsewhere, and the authors agreed tobacco probably kills more than the other 19 drugs combined. The scores are one panel's views, not measures.

items.statement: People who had taken more ecstasy showed less of a serotonin marker, in most studies.
items.why: Four studies found this link and two smaller ones didn't. But amounts came from memory, and people who take more ecstasy also take more of other drugs.

items.statement: In lab tests, men told their drink had vodka drank more, whatever was really in it.
items.why: They drank about twice as much in 15 minutes, while real vodka made no clear difference to how much they drank. These were lab tests from the 1970s and 1980s, with low blood alcohol.

items.statement: When meth's good feelings fade over days of use, the bad effects fade too.
items.why: In a small lab study, the good feelings were gone within three days, while dizziness, sickness and a pounding heart grew and appetite stayed down. Only six to nine people took part, on small doses.

items.statement: More people finish opioid withdrawal treatment on buprenorphine than on clonidine or lofexidine.
items.why: In 14 trials, about 72 in 100 finished on buprenorphine, against about 45 on the other medicines, and withdrawal was milder on average. No trial reported people coming off fentanyl.

items.statement: If an antidepressant mutes MDMA's effects, that means less MDMA is in your blood.
items.why: In small trials, two antidepressants lowered how strongly people rated MDMA's effects, yet the MDMA peak in their blood was about 15 to 18 percent higher. That's second-hand, from single trials of 16 healthy people each.

items.statement: In safety reports about ecstasy, cases that also named an antidepressant more often ended in death.
items.why: In US reports, those cases had about 1.6 times the odds of a fatal outcome, and reports naming muscle relaxants or anesthetics had higher odds still. These are voluntary reports, so they can't show cause, and nobody knows how many people took each mix.

items.statement: Children adopted away from a birth parent with a drug problem still have drug problems more often.
items.why: In a Swedish study, about 9 in 100 of them had one on record, against 4 in 100 when neither birth parent did. What birth parents pass on includes the pregnancy, not just genes.

items.statement: People who took GHB or GBL with alcohol more often ended up in critical care than those without.
items.why: Of emergency patients kept in hospital, 55 in 100 who'd also had alcohol went to critical care, against 22 in 100 without. Alcohol use was reported, not measured, and the amounts weren't known.

items.statement: In most published 'excited delirium' deaths, force such as restraint was recorded.
items.why: Force, including sedation and electrical weapons as well as restraint, was recorded in 94 of 104 deaths among published cases. These were selected reports, so they can't tell how much restraint, drugs or the agitated state caused a death.

items.statement: Colour test kits for MDMA are easy to read, even for first-timers.
items.why: In one small 2003 lab study, two people new to the kit made many mistakes: one missed both MDMA samples, and the other called four other drugs MDMA. Lab experts got MDMA right.

items.statement: In one study, people off heavy cannabis use for a year or more scored like people who hadn't used.
items.why: They scored no differently on any test, and a big review found smaller gaps in studies that asked people to stop for over 3 days. But few studies have followed people that long, and researchers disagree.

items.statement: People who microdose can't tell a real microdose from a dummy capsule.
items.why: In trials, people guessed right about 7 times in 10, and their ratings followed what they believed they'd taken. Feeling an effect may have shaped that belief.

items.statement: Police officers have had confirmed overdoses from just touching fentanyl.
items.why: None has been confirmed: a federal safety agency looked into cases where officers felt ill and found no signs of a serious overdose, though no officer had a test that finds fentanyl. Finding no proven case isn't proof it never happens.

items.reason: Dated trivia from groups studied 1985 to 2005; the death-rate fact already has a card, and these causes of death can't show what cocaine itself does.

items.statement: One dose of meth leaves people sadder and craving it the next morning.
items.why: In one small lab study, the biggest dose left people less alert and friendly the next morning than a dummy dose, but not sadder or more worried, and they didn't want meth more. Only eleven people took part, in a hospital unit.

items.statement: In one US survey, about 14 in 100 adults had alcohol use disorder in the past year.
items.why: Two or more of 11 signs of problem drinking in a year count, and about half the cases were mild. Another US survey found a little over half as many, so the number depends on the survey.

items.statement: Studies show people who drink a little live longer than people who never drank.
items.why: Many studies found slightly fewer deaths in people who drink a little, but compared with people who had never drunk, there was no clear difference. Few studies made that comparison, so a small gain or a small loss is still possible.

items.statement: In gene studies, drinking more went with more strokes, especially bleeding in the brain.
items.why: In a big study of Chinese adults, men whose genes made them drink more had more strokes, and bleeding strokes rose most. Women, who mostly don't drink, showed no link with the same genes.

items.statement: Early dementia can itself lead to benzodiazepine prescriptions.
items.why: Worry and poor sleep can come before dementia and lead to these prescriptions, and neither of two big studies could rule that out. In one, the authors said early symptoms may explain a small extra risk with light or moderate use.

items.statement: Caffeine doesn't really change how much you sleep that night.
items.why: Across 24 studies comparing nights with and without caffeine in the same people, they slept about 45 minutes less after caffeine, and their sleep was lighter. These were healthy adults with low to moderate usual intake, so heavy users, teenagers and older adults may differ.

items.statement: In small trials, cannabis medicines controlled sickness from chemotherapy better than a dummy did.
items.why: About 47 in 100 on a cannabis medicine had their sickness fully controlled, against 20 in 100 on a dummy. But only 102 people were in these three trials, and most trials in the review had serious weaknesses.

items.statement: When deaths were blamed on mephedrone, tests always found the drug in the body.
items.why: By October 2011, 128 deaths in the UK and nearby islands had been linked to it, and tests after death found none in 25. A negative test may miss earlier use, and a positive one doesn't prove cause.

items.statement: Levamisole, an animal worm medicine often found in cocaine around 2010, has been linked to blood and skin harm.
items.why: Case reports describe infection-fighting white blood cells falling very low, and painful purple skin patches, sometimes with dying skin. But since most cocaine held it, finding it shows exposure, not that it caused the harm, and how often harm happens is unknown.

items.statement: Making fentanyl test strips legal has been shown to cut drug deaths.
items.why: After the laws, deaths ran about 7 in 100 below the expected trend, but the study didn't check whether more people used strips, and the drop came in each law's very first month. Other changes at the same time could explain it.

items.statement: There's one agreed way to count a death as a drug death.
items.why: Lists use different rules, some counting drug poisoning as the main cause and others drugs found in tests. In Norway, only about 49 in 100 deaths were on both of two lists, and in Sweden fewer than half.

items.statement: Passing out from GHB again and again has been linked to worse memory.
items.why: In one Dutch study, people who had passed out many times remembered worse than people who used GHB regularly without passing out, and than people who used other drugs. It can't show GHB caused it, and nobody checked whether memory improves.

items.statement: People whose depression lifted on esketamine relapsed more often when switched to a dummy spray.
items.why: Of those switched to a dummy spray, 45 in 100 relapsed, against 27 in 100 who kept esketamine. The company behind it paid for the trials, and critics argue some relapses may be effects of stopping, which the trial couldn't tell apart.

items.statement: Ketamine drips for depression cause memory loss as often as ECT does.
items.why: In a Swedish trial, 19 of 90 had memory loss lasting over a day after ECT, against none of 91 after ketamine drips. Everyone knew which treatment they got.

items.statement: People who use ecstasy score worse on memory tests even if they use hardly any other drug.
items.why: In one study where breath, urine and hair tests checked that people used little else, memory scores didn't differ from others in the same all-night dance scene. Medium-sized differences couldn't be ruled out, and heavier use went with worse scores on one planning test.

items.statement: Bupropion and modafinil have been shown to help people stop using meth.
items.why: Across five trials, about 1 in 5 had stopped by the end, whether on medicine or a dummy pill. The trials were small, so a modest benefit or harm can't be ruled out.

items.statement: Brain scans prove that meth kills dopamine nerve cells.
items.why: Scans show less of one dopamine protein in people who used heavily, but it can drop without nerve cells dying, and other markers aren't always lower. Experts disagree, and nobody has shown it either way.

items.statement: Parkinson's disease is common in people diagnosed with meth or amphetamine problems.
items.why: In Utah health records of people with such diagnoses and no other drug or alcohol diagnosis, it was diagnosed about 3 times as often, but that's about 3 in 1,000 over about 7 years, against 1 in 1,000. Some diagnoses were probably other movement conditions.

items.statement: In most recent US overdose deaths involving meth, meth was the only drug.
items.why: Medical examiners' reports from 2021 to mid-2024 found fentanyl or other opioids in about 7 in 10 of these deaths. That's a different kind of record from the yearly death counts.

items.statement: The link between cannabis and car crashes stays just as strong when studies allow for drinking.
items.why: It shrinks: studies that allowed for alcohol found about 1.1 to 1.2 times the odds of a crash, against 1.7 to 1.8 in studies that didn't. These compare crashed drivers with others, so they can't show one driver's chance of crashing.

items.statement: In doctors' reports of harm from laughing gas, numbness or tingling was the most common problem.
items.why: Of 100 people in published reports, 80 had numbness or tingling and 58 had trouble walking. Not all used it for fun: 25 had been given it in surgery.

items.reason: Repeat: the answer's two cards already cover the fall in deaths near the site and why it isn't proof.
